content: The emergence of an international concern necessitates notification to the World Health Organization (WHO). Infection prevention and control (IPC) practices in healthcare settings must be implemented to ensure containment following such events. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized the importance of timely dissemination of surveillance reports to decision-makers at managerial or administrative levels and to frontline healthcare workers at the unit or ward level. Sharing these reports with all relevant stakeholders is critical to fostering organizational and behavioral changes as part of quality improvement efforts aimed at reducing healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and combating antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Reports should also be shared with safety and quality committees, as HAI data serve as a marker of healthcare quality. IPC activities should be tailored to the specific needs of healthcare facilities, based on the HAI situation and compliance with IPC practices. Facility-based surveillance systems play a vital role in the early detection of HAIs, identification of clusters and outbreaks, and assessment of the effectiveness of IPC interventions. High-quality data, including the proper application of case definitions and robust microbiological laboratory procedures, are essential for effective surveillance. These procedures are necessary for identifying etiological agents and AMR patterns, which have significant implications for patient care and IPC programs. A 2015 WHO survey on the global AMR situation revealed that many regions face challenges such as inadequate laboratory capacity, infrastructure, and data management, which hinder effective surveillance. The WHO Global AMR Surveillance System encourages the development of national AMR surveillance systems and recommends that countries utilize at least one externally quality-assured reference laboratory to support AMR surveillance. Laboratory capacity varies significantly across countries and regions, with the highest percentage of countries testing organisms for antibiotic sensitivity found in the Americas. However, many countries do not participate in external quality assessments to ensure the reliability of AMR data. National AMR surveillance reports are infrequent, except in two regions where most countries report on AMR surveillance. Additionally, an inventory of IPC national strategy or action plan documents revealed that while 79% of these documents provide guidance on surveillance priorities, only 52% address the need for standardized definitions. There are notable gaps in recommending surveillance in the context of outbreak response and detection. The GDG reviewed evidence to evaluate the impact of surveillance on HAIs. Hospital-based infection surveillance systems linked to national networks were associated with reduced rates of overall HAIs, central line-associated bloodstream infections, ventilator-associated pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and surgical site infections. For example, hospitals in the Dutch national surveillance network showed reduced HAI rates after four to five years of surveillance. Similarly, French ICU surveillance networks demonstrated a reduction in catheter-related bloodstream infections over five years. Active surveillance with public feedback as part of a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) bundle strategy was linked to decreased MRSA infections in a Singapore hospital. The GDG strongly believes that HAI surveillance is critical for evaluating and guiding IPC interventions, detecting and preventing HAIs and AMR, and improving healthcare quality. Based on the available evidence, the GDG strongly recommends facility-based HAI surveillance to guide IPC interventions and detect outbreaks, with timely feedback to healthcare workers, stakeholders, and national networks. The GDG acknowledges the inconsistent application of HAI standard definitions and highlights the need for research to identify and test alternative definitions suitable for low-resource settings. Research should also assess the reliability of surveillance based on patient records and hospital information systems. Furthermore, innovative surveillance technologies and the role of surveillance feedback in influencing behavioral change require further investigation. The GDG recognizes that implementing surveillance systems is resource-intensive, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Human resources, microbiological and laboratory support, information technology, and data management systems are critical for successful implementation. Despite these challenges, the GDG considers surveillance essential, not only for reducing HAIs but also for broader healthcare improvements. Clinical HAI surveillance can serve as a low-cost alternative in settings with limited microbiological support. Surveillance activities must balance the time required for IPC activities and the resources available. Feasibility varies across settings, but the GDG is confident that this recommendation can be implemented in all countries. Local human and laboratory resources, particularly in LMICs, must be evaluated and addressed. Additional education and training will likely be required to standardize audit and surveillance processes globally. The GDG is confident that key stakeholders will find this recommendation acceptable. Surveillance data must be adjusted for population case-mix and stratified by risk scores or indices to ensure accurate interpretation. In settings without access to quality laboratory services, process measurement and tracking, such as hand hygiene compliance, may provide useful alternatives. Reliable microbiological data are essential for early detection of pathogens, emerging AMR patterns, and understanding microbial spread, which are critical for IPC programs to implement appropriate transmission interruption procedures. In conclusion, the GDG strongly recommends facility-based HAI surveillance with timely feedback to guide IPC interventions, detect outbreaks, and improve healthcare quality. Research gaps, including the development of standardized HAI definitions and innovative surveillance technologies, must be addressed to enhance the effectiveness and feasibility of surveillance systems globally.
